title: LNK files, jump lists and shellbags
quick: LNK files, jump lists and shellbags are Windows traces of files and folders a user opened or browsed. They can show a file or folder existed even after it was deleted or the drive was removed.

sections.title: LNK files
text: An LNK file is a shortcut. Windows also makes them by itself when a user opens a file, and stores them in the user's Recent folder. The shortcut keeps details of its target: the path, the target's file times, its size and the volume serial number. For a network file it can keep share details.
The LNK can stay on disk after the target file is deleted, or after the USB drive holding it is gone.

sections.title: Jump lists
text: Jump lists are the recent and pinned items shown when you right-click a program on the taskbar. They are stored as automaticDestinations-ms and customDestinations-ms files in the user profile. They use the same data structure as LNK files and are tied to an application ID, so they show which program opened which file.

sections.title: Shellbags
text: Shellbags are registry entries that remember how a user viewed a folder in Windows Explorer, such as window size and sort order. As a side effect they list folders a user browsed. This includes folders on USB drives and network shares that are no longer connected. They are found in the user's NTUSER.DAT and UsrClass.dat hives.

example: A report says a user opened a secret document from a USB drive. The drive is not available. The examiner finds an LNK file and a jump list entry for the document with a volume serial number, and a shellbag for the same folder path.
mistakes: Assuming an LNK file means the user created it on purpose. Windows makes many automatically.
Using the LNK file's own times and the target times as if they were the same thing.
Thinking shellbags prove a folder's contents were seen. They show the folder was browsed.
Looking at only one of the three. They support each other.

terms.meaning: A Windows shortcut file with details of its target.
A list of recent or pinned files kept for each program.
A registry record of Explorer folder view settings that also shows browsed folders.
An ID of a file system volume, useful to link a file to a drive.

exam.q: Why can an LNK file prove a file once existed?
exam.a: It stores the target path, times and size, and the LNK often stays after the target is deleted.

exam.q: Name a trace of a folder on a removed USB drive.
exam.a: Shellbags. They keep the folder path even when the drive is not attached.
